Harness Engineering: The Discipline That Emerged Overnight

Stop trying to make your agent smarter. Make it more harnessed. A practitioner's field guide to the system that sits between a model and production.

By Maren Solás, originally published in Incredicorp Engineering, April 21, 2026

Harness engineering is new, and not new. As a practice, it has existed quietly wherever teams tried to make autonomous agents reliable. As a name, it is a few months old. But the shift it marks is real, and it is already changing how serious teams build with LLMs.

The model is the engine. The harness is everything else: the seatbelt, the steering, the dashboard, the guardrail. You don't drive the engine. You drive the car.

This is a short field guide to the discipline that emerged, quietly and all at once, in the first months of 2026. It does not sell a framework. It does not promise ten times the productivity. It describes what actually works when an autonomous agent has to run for hours, touch real systems, and not cause harm.

"The harness is everything in an AI agent except the model itself." — Martin Fowler, April 2026

1. A term, almost overnight

February 13, 2026. OpenAI published Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world, describing how its engineers built a one-million-line agent-first codebase where "humans interact with the system almost entirely through prompts."

March 2026. Anthropic posted the second of two connected papers explaining what it built to keep Claude working across long autonomous coding sessions. The discovery was not a smarter model but "a smarter environment around the model."

April 2, 2026. Martin Fowler published the definitive write-up. The formula that stuck: Agent = Model + Harness.

The word "harness" is doing real work. It implies restraint, yes, but also purpose: a horse wearing a harness is not a horse that is less free. It is a horse that is hitched to something, going somewhere.

What it is not

Confusion is expensive. Three disciplines keep getting collapsed together. They are not the same.

  • Not prompt engineering. Prompt engineering writes instructions for a single turn. Harness engineering builds the system that governs an agent across every turn.
  • Not model selection. The model is increasingly a commodity. The harness is the differentiator. Stanford's Meta-Harness work showed Haiku ranking higher than larger models purely through harness refinement.
  • Not orchestration alone. LangChain handles orchestration. Harness engineering encompasses the full control system, including what data the agent receives.

"It's no longer 'which framework should we use?' It's 'what does our harness look like?'" — Cobus Greyling

Why now: the 88 percent gap

88% of AI agent projects never reach production. That number has not improved as models have gotten more capable. The bottleneck is not the model. It is the absence of a production-grade harness.

27% of the failures trace back to data quality, what the agent is looking at, not to the model or the harness architecture itself. The lesson: harness is not a wrapper. It is a pipeline.

At the AI Engineer World's Fair in April 2026, three independent speakers named the "agent harness" and "context engineering" as the field's number-one next priority. The industry's attention moved, collectively, in about ten weeks.

If you are building an agent right now, the most useful thing you can do this quarter is not swap your model. It is to audit what surrounds your model. The rest of this article is how.

2. Anatomy of a harness

Most mature descriptions converge on the same four pieces. The names differ. The shape is the same.

01 - GUIDES System prompts, AGENTS.md, constraint files, personas, skeletons

02 - SENSORS Evals, validators, output parsers, drift detectors, LLM-as-judge

03 - DATA CONTEXT Repository-local artifacts, typed SDKs, lineage-verified sources

04 - ORCHESTRATION Sequences tasks, routes through gates

Most teams start at layer one, skip layer three, over-rotate on layer four, and ignore layer two entirely until production fails. The order of investment matters.

Layer 1: Guides

A guide directs what the agent knows and can do: system prompts, AGENTS.md files, constraint documents, schemas, persona specs. Think of guides as the agent's standing orders.

Anthropic's team documented "golden principles," opinionated, mechanical rules that keep the codebase legible and consistent for future agent runs. Two of theirs:

  • Prefer shared utility packages over hand-rolled helpers to keep invariants centralized.
  • Don't probe data "YOLO-style," validate boundaries or rely on typed SDKs so the agent can't accidentally build on guessed shapes.

Guides are boring to write. Write them anyway. They are the cheapest and most durable part of the harness.

# Persona, Context, Constraints (in/out), Evidence, Skeleton.

Persona: You are a staff reliability engineer.
         Cautious, concise, audit-first.

Context: User is on Pro plan, 12 seats,
         last invoice failed 2 days ago.
         Stripe customer_id: cus_123.

Constraints (must include):
  - One tool per turn.
  - Output JSON. Max 3 steps.
  - If refund > $500, require human_approval=true.

Constraints (must avoid):
  - Never expose full card number.
  - Never retry same tool > twice.

Evidence: Include confidence and reasoning for each step.

Skeleton: If tool fails twice, transition to failed
          and summarize.

Layer 2: Sensors

Sensors are evals, validation loops, output parsers, and drift detectors, the instruments that observe and verify agent behavior. Without sensors, the agent runs blind and you have no idea which run was the one that broke things.

Fowler distinguishes two kinds:

  • Computational — linters, schema checks, type probes. Cheap, fast, deterministic. Run on every change.
  • Inferential — semantic analysis, AI code review, LLM-as-judge. Slower and more expensive; results are more non-deterministic. Reserve for semantic judgment.

"The agent harness acts like a cybernetic governor, combining feed-forward and feedback to regulate the codebase toward its desired state." — Martin Fowler

Rule of thumb. If your agent touched something a human now has to review before it ships, you need a sensor there. Every review line is a missing sensor.

Layer 3: Data context

The certified, lineage-verified data the harness supplies to the agent at runtime. This is the layer teams most underestimate.

"From the agent's point of view, anything it can't access in-context while running effectively doesn't exist." — OpenAI Codex team

This line is the single most useful sentence in the whole practice. It forces a reframe: every decision about where information lives is now an architecture decision.

The Friday afternoon Slack thread where the team aligned on a pattern? Invisible to the agent. The Google Doc? Invisible. The senior engineer's head? Invisible. Push it into the repository, or accept that the agent doesn't know it.

Layer 4: Orchestration

Orchestration logic sequences agent tasks and routes outputs through review gates. This is the part that looks most like "regular" software, and that's why teams drown in it.

Anti-pattern: building a 40-node LangGraph before writing a 5-line AGENTS.md. Orchestration is downstream of guides and sensors. If the earlier layers are weak, the graph just routes bad behavior faster.

"Start simple. Build robust atomic tools. Let the model make the plan. Add guardrails, retries, and verification. That's harness engineering."

3. Context is the product

A harness without legible context is a harness around a blindfolded model. The agent does not have a tenure. It does not attend retros. Every run is a new hire with no memory of the last run.

"Our human engineers' goal was making it possible for an agent to reason about the full business domain directly from the repository itself." — OpenAI Codex team

That is the bar. A new agent, given only the repo, should be able to understand what to do and why. This is expensive up front. It is also the only investment whose returns compound every time you run the agent.

Checklist: a legible repo

  • AGENTS.md at the root, kept current.
  • Executable plans checked in as markdown, not in tickets.
  • Schemas before prose; prose that references schemas.
  • ADRs for every non-obvious decision.
  • README files named for what agents will search.
  • No "tribal" knowledge left verbal.

The Friday cleanup used to cost OpenAI's team twenty percent of the week. They replaced it with background Codex tasks that scan for deviations and open targeted refactor PRs, most auto-merged in under a minute.

Golden principles: opinionated, mechanical, enforced

Golden principles are rules that keep the codebase legible across agent runs. The three qualities matter in that order.

  • Opinionated. Pick one pattern. Not "we could use either." An agent without a house style invents its own, and styles diverge across files.
  • Mechanical. The rule must be checkable by a script or an LLM judge. "Write clean code" is not a golden principle. "Prefer typed SDKs; fail CI if a file imports requests directly" is.
  • Enforced. Either the rule runs on every PR, or it does not exist. A principle without a sensor is a suggestion.

"When something failed, the fix was almost never 'try harder.'" — OpenAI Codex team

The next thought was always: what capability is missing, and how do we make it legible and enforceable for the agent? That is the cycle to internalize.

4. Seven patterns that hold

These are not the only patterns. They are the ones every working harness in 2026 seems to converge on, regardless of model or stack.

Pattern 01: Persona

A persona is not flavor text. It is a role definition that collapses ambiguity. "You are a staff reliability engineer. Cautious, concise, audit-first." Those three adjectives narrow a thousand downstream decisions. Pick personas with verbs you want; avoid vague adjectives like helpful, friendly, expert.

Heuristic: if two engineers reading the persona would draw different code from it, rewrite it until they wouldn't.

Pattern 02: Dual constraints

Write must include and must avoid separately. Humans read the positive list. Agents obey the negative one.

must_include:
  - One tool per turn.
  - Output JSON. Max 3 steps.
  - If refund > $500: require human_approval.

must_avoid:
  - Never expose full card.
  - Never retry same tool > 2x.
  - Never fabricate customer IDs.

This structure takes three minutes to write. The agent running under it caused no production incident across four months.

Pattern 03: Self-interrogation

Before an agent gets loose on production, ask it to list the edge cases a senior engineer would test. One practitioner, building a refund agent, ran exactly this prompt and discovered a partial-refund-plus-currency-switch case the team had missed. It would have cost real money.

Pattern 04: Reflection

Reflection is the agent seeing the results of its actions and reasoning about them. Did the tool call succeed? Was the output what it expected? Is there a cheaper route?

Without reflection, the agent is a Roomba bumping a wall forever. With reflection, it is a Roomba that eventually tries a different room. Reflection is not free, every reflection step is another model call. Cap the depth.

Pattern 05: Skeleton

A skeleton is a flow specification the agent must fill in, not invent. State transitions. Failure transitions. Exit conditions. Writing the skeleton separately from the code is the difference between a prototype that works on a good day and a system that survives a bad one.

# Skeleton for the refund agent

start -> plan -> (tool_ok | tool_fail)
tool_fail -> retry (max 2) -> fail
plan -> execute -> reflect
reflect -> (done | refine)
refine -> plan  (max depth 3)
any -> human_handoff if risk > H

Pattern 06: Deliberate memory

The agent's long-term memory stores past successes, failures, and crucial rules, so it doesn't make the same mistake twice. The word that matters is deliberate. Dumping a vector DB full of every past conversation is not memory. It is a landfill.

Ask two questions for every memory entry:

  1. What behavior change does this memory enable?
  2. What expiry or override does it need?

Pattern 07: Mandatory traces

A trace is a record of what the agent did, what it saw, and why it chose what it chose. Top teams maintain mandatory traces on every run, not sampled, not optional. Non-negotiable because the bugs that matter are the ones you cannot reproduce. If a trace does not exist, the incident may as well not have happened.

A trace should include, at minimum: the guide version, every tool call and its result, every model call with inputs and outputs, every sensor verdict with reason, confidence scores, and the final action and who or what approved it.

"The boring stuff that doesn't make it into a Twitter thread." — Neil Dave, on what top teams actually do

5. Where harnesses fail

A short, practical catalogue. Most production failures are not exotic. They are four or five patterns, repeated.

Failure 01: The quiet one

Twenty-seven percent of agent project failures trace to data quality, not model limitations. This is the failure that looks like everything else. The agent gave a wrong answer. The prompt was right. The tools were right. The guardrails fired. And still: wrong.

The cause is almost always upstream. Stale data. Mislabeled columns. A join that silently dropped rows. The agent reasoned correctly over the wrong inputs.

Diagnostic: when the agent is wrong and you can't explain it, check the data layer before you touch the prompt. Ninety percent of "prompt engineering" is really data engineering in disguise.

Failure 02: Tool sprawl

Every tool you add expands the agent's reachable state space. "Swapped models, added a vector DB, gave it twelve tools. The demo was magic. In production it was a toddler with a credit card."

Twelve tools is too many. Usually. Start with three. Earn the fourth by showing it replaces, not supplements, an existing flow. Never add a tool without adding a constraint.

Failure 03: Runaway loops

The classic: agent tries X, X fails, agent retries X, X fails, agent retries X. Sometimes with more expensive models. Sometimes forever.

# Always ship these three caps

max_steps_per_turn: 3
max_retries_per_tool: 2
max_total_cost_usd: 2.50

# On cap hit:
on_cap_exceeded: human_handoff with trace & reason

These three caps are cheap to write and have outsized protective power. They are the fire extinguisher in the kitchen. You hope you never use them.

Failure 04: Drift

Drift is what happens between model versions, between quarterly refactors, between the day you wrote the prompt and the day you are debugging it. The agent still works. It just works slightly differently. And nobody noticed.

"Even the most polished AI agents fail most consistently on long-running autonomous tasks." — on Anthropic's harness research

Drift canaries, a starter set:

  • 20 canonical user inputs, frozen.
  • The agent's last-known-good response for each.
  • A similarity threshold, per input.
  • A daily cron that reruns all 20.
  • An alert on any diff above threshold.

Twenty inputs, one cron, one alert. That's the whole mechanism. Teams that have this sleep better. Teams that don't are surprised at least once a quarter.

6. A thirty-day practice

Everything above is useless if it stays abstract. Here is a concrete plan. Four weeks, from your first harness to your first production-worthy one.

Week 01: Audit

  • List every place your current agent gets context. Every one.
  • Mark which are repository-local. The rest is invisible to the agent.
  • Write a one-page AGENTS.md summarizing the rules a new agent needs to know.
  • Do one self-interrogation run. Write down what it surfaces.

Deliverable: a single file a new engineer (or agent) could read in five minutes and get the gist.

Week 02: Constrain

  • Write the persona. Three adjectives, not ten.
  • List must-includes. List must-avoids. Keep them short.
  • Add the three caps: steps, retries, cost.
  • Define the skeleton state machine on one page.

Deliverable: a single harness.md, under 200 lines, checked into the repo.

Week 03: Observe

  • Add one computational sensor per golden principle. Fail CI on violation.
  • Add one inferential sensor: an LLM judge for the three riskiest outputs.
  • Enable mandatory traces. Store them. Grep them.
  • Set up 20 drift canaries and a daily cron.

Week 04: Feed back

  • Every failed trace becomes either a new test or a new golden principle.
  • Every human correction gets logged as a memory entry, with an expiry.
  • Every drift alert gets a quick triage within 24 hours.
  • Schedule a weekly 30-minute review of the harness. Not the agent: the harness.

The finish line. End of week four: an agent that can run a full workflow, unsupervised, under its own harness, with traces a human can audit in five minutes. That is not impressive in 2026. It is table stakes. Now you ship.

The craft of subtraction

The most interesting finding in a year of harness research was not a new framework. It was the shape of the answer when researchers treated the harness itself as an optimization target.

"A fascinating craft of subtraction, adding value by removing complication." The good harness is not the one with the most guards. It is the one with the fewest necessary guards, each earning its place.

Stop trying to make your agent smarter. Make it more harnessed.

The intelligence is already there. It just needs rails. Build the rails. Write them down. Measure them. Throw away the ones that don't earn their place.

That's the whole practice.
